revenue.question: Revenue grew from $80m to $100m. What was the growth rate?
revenue.hint: Divide the increase by the previous revenue, then multiply by 100.
revenue.explanation: (100 − 80) / 80 × 100 = 25%. Use the previous period as the denominator.

gross-margin.question: Revenue is $100m and direct costs are $60m. What is gross margin?
gross-margin.hint: First subtract direct costs from revenue. Then divide by revenue.
gross-margin.explanation: (100 − 60) / 100 × 100 = 40%. Each revenue dollar leaves $0.40 before operating expenses.

fcf.question: Operating cash flow is $24m and capital spending is $9m. What is free cash flow?
fcf.hint: Subtract capital spending from operating cash flow.
fcf.explanation: 24 − 9 = $15m. This simplified FCF measure deducts capital spending; it is not the same as net income.

operating-margin.question: Gross profit is $40m, operating expenses are $25m, and revenue is $100m. What is operating margin?
operating-margin.hint: Subtract operating expenses from gross profit, then divide by revenue.
operating-margin.explanation: (40 − 25) / 100 × 100 = 15%. Operating expenses reduce the amount left from gross profit.

roic.question: NOPAT is $12m and average invested capital is $80m. What is ROIC?
roic.hint: Divide NOPAT by average invested capital.
roic.explanation: 12 / 80 × 100 = 15%. Compare this return with the cost of capital and with comparable businesses.

net-debt.question: Debt is $50m and cash is $20m. What is net debt?
net-debt.explanation: 50 − 20 = $30m. Also examine debt maturities and whether cash is available to repay debt.

pe.question: Market capitalization is $180m and annual net income is $12m. What is P/E?
pe.hint: Divide market capitalization by net income.
pe.explanation: 180 / 12 = 15×. This multiple alone does not establish whether the company is cheap.

present-value.question: You expect $110 one year from now. At a 10% discount rate, what is its present value?
present-value.explanation: 110 / 1.10 = $100. Discounting converts a future cash flow into a value today.

sensitivity.question: In a DCF with unchanged positive cash flows and terminal growth, what happens when the discount rate increases?
sensitivity.hint: A larger discount rate reduces the present value of future cash flows.
sensitivity.explanation: Estimated value falls. Test a range of discount rates because one valuation result can conceal substantial uncertainty.

margin-of-safety.question: Conservative estimated value is $100 per share and the price is $70. What is the margin of safety?
margin-of-safety.hint: Divide the discount by estimated value, not by price.
margin-of-safety.explanation: (100 − 70) / 100 × 100 = 30%. Upside from the price is about 42.9%; it uses a different denominator.

owner-earnings.question: Net income is $20m, D&A is $6m, maintenance CapEx is $8m, and required working capital increases by $2m. With no other adjustments, what are owner earnings?
owner-earnings.hint: Add D&A to net income, then subtract maintenance spending and the working-capital increase.
owner-earnings.explanation: 20 + 6 − 8 − 2 = $16m. Maintenance spending is an estimate; assess a range and keep the reinvestment consistent with the growth forecast.

normalized-earnings.question: Reported earnings are $30m, including an $8m asset-sale gain and a genuine one-time $3m closure cost. Both items are after tax. What are adjusted earnings before cycle analysis?
normalized-earnings.hint: Remove the unusual gain and add back the unusual cost.
normalized-earnings.explanation: 30 − 8 + 3 = $25m. This does not finish normalization: assess the economic cycle and whether the excluded cost really is exceptional.

capital-allocation.question: Management repurchases shares. Which evidence best supports the claim that this creates value?
choices: EPS rises after the share count falls
Shares are bought below a well-supported value estimate while retaining adequate liquidity
The repurchase is larger than last year
capital-allocation.hint: Consider the price paid, available alternatives, and the company’s remaining financial capacity.
capital-allocation.explanation: Price and financial capacity matter. Higher EPS alone does not establish value creation; also compare repurchases with other uses of capital.

value-trap.question: Which situation provides the strongest evidence of a possible value trap?
choices: A sound business stays below a credible value estimate without a near-term catalyst
A share price falls while operating performance remains stable
A low P/E uses peak profits while customers leave permanently and replacement spending is deferred
value-trap.hint: Look for lasting damage to earning power or assets, not a delay in market recognition alone.
value-trap.explanation: Lost customers and deferred necessary spending can undermine the earnings used in the valuation. A missing catalyst alone does not establish a value trap.

paths.title: Read financial statements
paths.summary: Follow revenue through profit and cash generation.

paths.title: Assess a business
paths.summary: Connect profitability, capital efficiency, and debt.

paths.title: Think like a business owner
paths.summary: Estimate earning power, assess capital allocation, and avoid apparent bargains with weak economics.

traces.title: Gross margin
traces.why: Calculate gross profit from revenue and direct costs, then divide by revenue.

traces.title: Free cash flow
traces.why: Use operating cash flow, then deduct capital spending. Net income is not the starting figure.

traces.title: Net debt
traces.why: Both figures come from the balance sheet at the same date.

chapters.title: Does growth produce profit?
chapters.prompt: What else would you inspect before calling this a strong business?
chapters.model: Revenue increased by 25% and gross margin is 40%. Those figures alone do not establish business quality. Compare margins over time, customer retention, and competitors. Operating profit is $15m after operating expenses.

chapters.title: Does profit turn into cash?
chapters.prompt: What could make this year’s cash flow look stronger than its lasting cash generation?
chapters.model: Free cash flow is $15m, above net income of $12m. Inspect working-capital movements and deferred capital spending. Net debt is $30m; debt maturities and available cash also matter.

chapters.title: What does the price assume?
chapters.prompt: What would you need to know before deciding whether 15× earnings is attractive?
chapters.model: P/E is 15×, but the multiple cannot settle the valuation. Check earnings durability, growth needs, peer differences, and debt. Test downside assumptions and write down what would invalidate your thesis.
